title: The stolen mango
hookLine: is the thief responsible for mangoes that grew from the one he took? yes (Milinda, Book 2)
last: OWING ITS LIGHT TO THE ONE BEFORE.

lines: A FRESH FLAME, A FRESH START?
A FARMER, A THIEF, A KING.
cards: Here's the loophole the king spots. If the one reborn is neither the same nor another, maybe the new one gets off clean. A fresh flame, a fresh start.
Why answer for what an earlier flame did? It sounds like a legal argument, and Nagasena answers it like one. He takes the king into a courtroom.
A farmer drags a man before the king: this man stole my mangoes. And the thief has a clever defense ready.

teach.h: THESE AREN'T THE MANGOES HE PLANTED.
teach.b: First, the defense. Your majesty, the thief says, I never took the mangoes this man planted. He put a mango in the ground; the ones I picked grew on the tree that came up from it.
Different mangoes. Not guilty. Second, the verdict.
Would that man deserve punishment? Nagasena asks. Yes, says the king: whatever he says, the mangoes he took grew from the one the farmer planted.
Third, the turn. Just so, Nagasena says. A person does good or bad in this life, and from those deeds another name and form is born.
So the deeds are not escaped.

The new life grew from the old the way the fruit grew from the planted mango. He gives the king more cases of the same shape. A man lights a fire in the cold season to warm himself and walks off without putting it out.
It spreads and burns a neighbor's field.

teach.h: A FIRE LEFT BURNING, A FIELD LOST.
teach.b: The fire I lit, he says, isn't the fire that burned your field. Responsible anyway, says the king, because one fire came from the other. Fourth, what this keeps together.
Yesterday's flame said nothing fixed passes across. Today's mango says that doesn't make you a stranger to your own past. Both stand at once.
In this passage, kamma isn't pictured as a judge handing out sentences from outside.

teach.h: KAMMA: FRUIT FROM WHAT WAS PLANTED.
teach.b: It's fruit growing from what was planted; no one needs to carry it from the seed.
And it grows on any ordinary day, not only across lives: the word said yesterday, the promise left lying, the fire not put out.

how: Buddhist teachers use Nagasena's mango and fire cases to explain kamma and rebirth together: no fixed self passes across, yet a life is not cut off from the deeds it grew from.

o: a reward the king gives to honest farmers
a fresh fruit with no tie to the old seed
fruit grown from a planted seed, so still yours

games.q: the stolen mango: tap the pairs.
p: these aren't the mangoes he planted
fruit growing from what was planted

s: Nagasena says the reborn one gets a clean slate
his mango case says the opposite: the new life grows from the deeds of the old, so they aren't escaped.
the king rules the mango thief guilty
the mangoes he took grew from the one the farmer planted.
the man who left the fire burning is excused because it was a different fire
the king says he's responsible, because one fire came from the other.

games.q: you're the king. a thief says he never took the farmer's mangoes, only fruit from a tree that grew from them. what's your verdict?
o: guilty. they grew from the farmer's.
games.why: the king says guilty, and Nagasena springs the point: just so, a new life grows from the deeds of the old one.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing that happened because of something you did, kind or careless: a message you sent, a door you held, or didn't.
Don't argue the case or build a clever defense; just let it be yours, this grew from that, held without excuse and without punishment.

wordCard.voice: Mango. Nagasena's courtroom case: the thief is guilty, because the fruit he took grew from the one that was planted.

orig.note: Pali: mango. the fruit in Nagasena's courtroom case.

carryVoice: Your line: the mango grew from yours. Not a sentence handed down, but fruit from a seed. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 2 (the mango thief and the fire left burning)
